cards.text: Proverbs starts a new section here, and the writer talks right to the listener: "Incline your ear and hear the words of the wise…" Then he adds, "…apply your mind to my knowledge…" Friend, that's the oldest way I know of saying PUT THE PHONE DOWN.

cards.question: The writer says it's pleasing to keep these words within you and also on your lips.

cards.text: Then the writer gets personal: "…I instruct you today—yes, you." YES, YOU, friend, not whoever's on mute in the meeting pretending their camera's broken.

cards.question: The writer says all this instruction has a goal. What is it?

answers.text: So your trust may be in the LORD
So your name will be remembered
So your barns will be full

cards.text: The writer has written thirty sayings about counsel and knowledge, to show true and reliable words. I've got ONE saying, "don't open the oven every two minutes," and friend, I can't even keep THAT one.

cards.question: These true and reliable words will help you soundly answer whom?

cards.text: Then the writer's next words stand up for the little guy: "Do not rob a poor man because he is poor, and do not crush the afflicted at the gate…"

cards.question: Don't rob the poor or crush the afflicted at the gate, because the ___ will take up their case.

cards.text: And the LORD will plunder those who rob them. Next saying: do not make friends with an angry man, and do not associate with a hot-tempered man.

cards.question: Why steer clear of the hot-tempered man, the guy who honks for three straight miles when somebody cuts him off?

answers.text: You may learn his ways and get caught in a snare
He may turn his anger on you someday
You may lend him money and never get it back

cards.text: Here's one for your wallet: do not be one who gives pledges, who puts up security for debts. Somebody slides that paper across the table and says "it's just a formality," and friend, it is NEVER just a formality.

cards.question: If you put up security for a debt and have nothing to pay with, what does the writer say could be taken?

answers.text: Your own bed from under you
Your seat at the city gate

cards.text: Next the writer turns to the land, and an ancient boundary stone your fathers placed. That rock has been sitting there longer than my oldest joke, and friend, that's a LONG time.

cards.question: The writer says moving an ancient boundary stone your fathers placed is fine if you need more room.

cards.text: Then the writer asks, "Do you see a man skilled in his work?" Friend, I've been stamping cookies a LONG time, and I still smudge one every batch.

cards.question: A man skilled in his work won't stand before obscure men. He'll be stationed in the presence of ___.

cards.text: Next up, dinner with a ruler: consider carefully what is set before you, and if you possess a great appetite, put a knife to your throat. Friend, that's not a dinner tip, that's a WARNING LABEL.

cards.question: At the ruler's table, why shouldn't you crave his delicacies?

answers.text: That food is for his servants
That food is set aside for later

cards.text: And now the writer talks money, and how hard to chase it. Lean in, friend, this one's for everybody who's ever said "just one more shift."

cards.question: The writer says it's worth wearing yourself out to get rich.

cards.text: Then the writer says, "…be wise enough to restrain yourself." And he paints a wild picture, friend: money with WINGS.

cards.question: Wealth makes wings for itself and flies like an eagle to the sky. What's the point of that picture?

answers.text: Riches come to whoever chases them

cards.text: I've SEEN that eagle, friend: it hits the account Friday, and by Sunday it's waving down from the clouds like BYE. Then the writer turns to a stingy man's table: do not eat his bread, and do not crave his delicacies.

cards.question: The stingy host says "Eat and drink," but what's really going on inside him?

answers.text: He's hoping you'll stay all night
He's getting ready to ask a favor

cards.text: His heart is not with you. It's the friend who says "Grab anything you want!" and then sends you a payment request for ONE cookie.

cards.question: After you vomit up what little you've eaten at the stingy man's table, the writer says your pleasant words go to waste.

cards.text: Then comes a quick one, short enough to stamp on a cookie: do not speak to a fool.

cards.question: Don't speak to a fool, for he will ___ the wisdom of your words.
The boundary stone warning comes back, with something added: don't encroach on the fields of the ___.
Leave the fields of the fatherless alone, because their Redeemer will take up their case against you. What does the writer say about their Redeemer?

cards.text: Then the writer says, "Apply your heart to instruction and your ears to words of knowledge." Back at the start it was ear and mind, and now it's heart and ears.

cards.question: The last saying here turns to raising a child. The writer says to hold back discipline from a child.

cards.text: The writer goes on, "…although you strike him with a rod, he will not die." Then he says, "Strike him with a rod, and you will deliver his soul from Sheol."
And that's where I'll set the stamp down for now, friend. These thirty sayings aren't all said yet.
